title: The Stones of Venice
description: Published in three volumes between 1851 and 1853 and the central work of Ruskin's middle period: a history of Venetian architecture and a moral history of the Venetian republic that becomes, in the chapter 'The Nature of Gothic', a criticism of industrial labour.
plot_or_argument: Volume I treats the foundations and the Byzantine style, Volume II the Gothic palaces and the 'Nature of Gothic' chapter, Volume III the Renaissance and the fall of Venice; the argument is that the decline of Venetian architecture follows the decline of Venetian faith and that the workers of the Gothic cathedral were free men while those of the Renaissance were slaves.
literary_form: Architectural and social criticism in three volumes
historical_context: The 1848 revolutions and the siege of Venice, the Victorian Gothic Revival, and the pre-Raphaelite critique of industrial labour; the book was read by Morris at Oxford in 1853 and changed his life.
literary_significance: The Stones of Venice is the founding text of the social criticism of art: 'The Nature of Gothic' gave Morris and the Arts and Crafts movement their central doctrine that good art depends on the free labour of the craftsman, and through Morris it shaped the socialism of the 1880s and the twentieth-century theory of design.

title: Unto This Last: Four Essays on the First Principles of Political Economy
description: Four essays published in the Cornhill Magazine in 1860 under the title 'Unto This Last' (the parable of the labourers in the vineyard) and collected as a book in 1862: the most influential attack on classical political economy in English.
plot_or_argument: Ruskin argues that the 'economic man' of Ricardo and Mill is a fiction, that wealth is not the accumulation of commodities but the possession of 'things that are useful and life-giving', that the 'illth' produced by commerce is a real cost, and that the just wage and the responsibility of the employer are moral duties. He proposes a guild of labourers and an education for the poor.
historical_context: The 1860 Cornhill controversy (Thackeray, the editor, stopped the series after the fourth essay), the Lancashire cotton famine of 1861-65, and the socialist and Christian-socialist movements of the 1880s.
literary_significance: Unto This Last is the most influential English work of moral economics: Gandhi read it in 1904 and said it 'captured' him and led him to the doctrine of the 'welfare of all'; Attlee and the founders of the British Labour Party took their moral vocabulary from it, and it is the founding text of the twentieth-century critique of economics as a value-free science.

title: Sesame and Lilies
description: Two lectures delivered in Manchester and Dublin in 1864 and published in 1865: 'Of Kings' Treasuries' on reading and education, and 'Of Queens' Gardens' on the education of women, the most widely read of all Ruskin's writings.
plot_or_argument: 'Of Kings' Treasuries' argues that true reading is an act of attention and obedience to the author, and that a nation's education consists in its libraries and its reading; 'Of Queens' Gardens' argues that women should be educated to a 'queenly' influence in the home, and its conservative ideal of womanhood provoked a long controversy.
historical_context: The 1860s, the movement for women's higher education (Girton, 1869; Newnham, 1871), and Ruskin's own lectures at the Working Men's College.
literary_significance: Sesame and Lilies was the most widely read of Ruskin's books and the one that made him a public educator; 'Of Queens' Gardens' became a central text in the Victorian debate on women's education, and its ideal of 'queenly' domesticity was the target of the New Woman argument of the 1890s. The essays are the classic English statements of the moral value of reading.

title: Praeterita: Outlines of Scenes and Thoughts Perhaps Worthy of Memory in My Past Life
description: Ruskin's autobiography, serialised in the magazine of the same name in twenty-four parts from 1885 and left unfinished in 1889: the most beautiful of Victorian autobiographies, and the retrospective re-creation of a childhood, a family and a Europe before the railway.
plot_or_argument: The narrative moves from the London house of his childhood and the sherry business of his father to the Continental tours of 1833-1845, his mother and father, his first love and his marriage, his work on Modern Painters and the Stones of Venice, and the death of his parents; the last chapters are fragmentary and haunted.
historical_context: The 1880s, Ruskin's failing mind and the death of his parents, and the Victorian vogue for autobiography (Mill, Darwin, Trollope, Newman).
literary_significance: Praeterita is the finest Victorian autobiography after Mill's and the model for the twentieth-century literary memoir; its reconstruction of childhood perception and its refusal of the conventional pieties made it a central text for Pater, Proust and the modern autobiography, and its unfinished condition is itself a document of the age.
attribution_notes: Unfinished: Ruskin wrote twenty-four chapters of a projected longer work and abandoned it in 1889 as his mental health failed; the published text is what he left.

title: A System of Logic, Ratiocinative and Inductive
description: Published in 1843 and the foundational work of English empiricist philosophy of science: an account of the methods of induction, of the logic of the moral sciences, and of the errors of the a priori school.
plot_or_argument: The six books treat names and propositions, reasoning, induction, the operations subsidiary to induction, the fallacies, and the logic of the moral sciences. The central contribution is the formulation of the 'methods of experimental inquiry' — agreement, difference, residues and concomitant variations — and the argument that the moral sciences must be deductive in method but cannot predict individual conduct.
historical_context: The 1830s-40s, the Scottish philosophy of Thomas Brown and Dugald Stewart, Whewell's and Herschel's philosophy of science, and the controversy with the intuitionist school of Coleridge and Hamilton.
literary_significance: The System of Logic established the empiricist philosophy of science in English and gave the social sciences their methodological foundation; its 'methods of inquiry' are still the standard formulation, and its sixth book founded the modern logic of the social sciences.

title: Principles of Political Economy, with Some of Their Applications to Social Philosophy
description: Published in 1848 and the standard English economics text for a generation: a systematic restatement of the classical political economy that opened the way for reform by distinguishing the laws of production from the arrangements of distribution.
plot_or_argument: The five books treat production, distribution (property, wages, profits, rent), exchange (value, money, international trade), the progress of society, and the influence of government, including the case for the taxation of unearned increments, the reform of land tenure, and the stationary state as a possible good rather than a disaster.
historical_context: The 1847 crisis and the Irish famine, the Chartist and cooperative movements, the land question, and the socialist criticisms of Louis Blanc and the English Owenites.
literary_significance: The Principles taught political economy to the English-speaking world (the first edition sold out in a year) and made the distinction between production and distribution the basis of the reformist economics that led to the welfare state; Mill's discussion of the stationary state and the environment is the founding text of ecological economics.

title: On Liberty
description: Published in 1859 with the dedication to Harriet Taylor Mill, and the single most influential defence of individual freedom in the English language: the argument that the only justification for coercing an individual is to prevent harm to others.
plot_or_argument: The five chapters treat the history of liberty and the tyranny of opinion, the liberty of thought and discussion, individuality as one of the elements of well-being, the limits of the authority of society over the individual, and applications of the doctrine to education and the state.
historical_context: The 1850s, the growth of Victorian public opinion and the 'despotism of custom', the temperance and sabbatarian legislation, and Mill's own collaboration with Harriet Taylor.
literary_significance: On Liberty gave liberalism its central principle and its most quoted defence of free speech ('If all mankind minus one were of one opinion...'); it is a foundation text of modern democratic theory and civil liberties law, and it remains the reference point for the debate on the limits of state action.

title: Utilitarianism
description: Serialised in Fraser's Magazine in 1861 and published in 1863: the classic statement of the utilitarian ethics of the greatest happiness principle, with the influential distinction between higher and lower pleasures.
plot_or_argument: The five chapters treat the question of utility, the 'proof' of the principle (that the only evidence of desirability is actual desire), the ultimate sanction of the principle in the social feelings, the proof of the principle, and the connection between justice and utility.
historical_context: The 1860s, the critique of utilitarianism by Whewell, Hamilton and Carlyle, and the social reform movements that Mill hoped to ground in a philosophical ethics.
literary_significance: Utilitarianism is the definitive formulation of the ethics that the Victorian age inherited from Bentham and Mill's father, and the higher/lower pleasures distinction gave modern moral philosophy one of its central arguments; the justice chapter is still the starting point for the modern debate on punishment and rights.

title: The Subjection of Women
description: Published in 1869, written in collaboration with Harriet Taylor and dedicated to her: the most rigorous philosophical argument for the equality of women in the nineteenth century, and the text that the Victorian women's movement took as its manifesto.
plot_or_argument: Mill argues that the subjection of women is a relic of the past preserved by custom, that the evidence of women's inferiority is worthless because it is drawn from a state of constrained development, that the legal ownership of wives under coverture is a form of slavery, that women should be enabled to choose any profession, and that marriage should become a partnership of equals.
historical_context: The 1860s and the campaign for women's suffrage, the Married Women's Property Acts of 1870 and 1882, and the parliamentary debate on the Second Reform Act in which Mill proposed the inclusion of women.
literary_significance: The Subjection of Women is the founding document of modern liberal feminism and remains the classic philosophical statement of the case: it gave the nineteenth-century women's movement its intellectual authority, and its analysis of the 'custom' and the 'nature' argument is still the core of the modern debate.
attribution_notes: Published under Mill's name; he states in the Autobiography and in the dedication that the book was an embodiment of his wife's ideas and the result of their collaboration, and modern scholarship (Hayek, Rose, and the Oxford edition) treats Harriet Taylor Mill's share as substantial.

title: Considerations on Representative Government
description: Published in February 1861: Mill's systematic account of the best form of representative government, and the most sophisticated Victorian treatment of the relation of the educated few to the democratic multitude.
plot_or_argument: The book treats the criteria for a good form of government, the two principles of participation and competence, the extension of the franchise and the representation of minorities by proportional voting (the 'Hare' scheme), the reform of the House of Lords, the dangers of class legislation and the role of the civil service.
historical_context: The 1860s, the Second Reform Act of 1867, the parliamentary reform agitation, and the American Civil War as a test of democratic government.
literary_significance: Considerations on Representative Government is the central Victorian contribution to democratic theory; its proposal of proportional representation and of a plural vote for the educated gave the twentieth century two of its most enduring institutional ideas, and its analysis of democracy's mediocrity was taken up by Arnold and by the modern critics of mass society.

title: Autobiography
description: Written in the 1850s and revised in the 1860s, and published posthumously by Mill's stepdaughter Helen Taylor in 1873: the most discussed autobiography of the Victorian period, and the record of the education that produced its author and of the crisis that nearly destroyed him.
plot_or_argument: The chapters follow Mill's extraordinary education by his father, his work at the East India Company, the mental crisis of 1826-27 and his recovery through poetry (Wordsworth, particularly), his discovery of Harriet Taylor, his political and philosophical development, his parliamentary career, and his estimate of the age.
historical_context: The 1820s-60s, the utilitarian circle, the Benthamites and the Edinburgh Review, and the Victorian crisis of faith and of the reformist confidence.
literary_significance: The Autobiography is a central document of Victorian intellectual history and of the theory of education: its account of the 'crisis' in which a man educated only in analysis finds himself with no feeling left is the classic case of the dangers of a purely rational education, and its portrait of Harriet Taylor made her a figure in the history of English feminism.

title: Apologia Pro Vita Sua
description: Published in eight parts in 1864-65 in answer to Charles Kingsley's charge that he had taught that truth need not be kept with heretics: the greatest Victorian religious autobiography, and the book that restored Newman's reputation and made his name.
plot_or_argument: The Apologia narrates the development of Newman's religious opinions from his Evangelical childhood through the Oxford Movement, the Tracts for the Times, Tract 90, the move to Rome and the Oratory; the argument is that his changes were not inconsistencies but a coherent development under an authority he could not resist.
literary_form: Spiritual autobiography (in seven parts, with a supplementary chapter)
historical_context: The 1864 controversy with Kingsley and the pages of Macmillan's and the Birmingham Oratory's pamphlet, the Oxford Movement's memory, and the position of Catholics in Victorian England after the restoration of the hierarchy in 1850.
literary_significance: The Apologia created the modern spiritual autobiography and is the most persuasive account in English of the grounds of religious belief; it is also the central historical document of the Oxford Movement, and its prose is the standard against which Victorian religious writing is measured.

title: The Idea of a University
description: The lectures delivered in Dublin in 1852 as rector of the new Catholic University, revised and collected with additional essays in 1873: the classic English defence of liberal education, and the source of the modern idea of the university.
plot_or_argument: Newman argues that knowledge is its own end, that the university is a place of teaching universal knowledge rather than of research or of professional training, that theology must be included among the sciences, and that the educated gentleman is the product of a liberal education; the later essays add the argument for the study of literature.
literary_form: Lectures and essays (Dublin, 1852; collected 1873 with the 1858 essays)
historical_context: The 1850s, the founding of the Catholic University of Ireland (1854) and the Oxford debates on the relation of university to Church, and the Victorian controversy over useful versus liberal knowledge (Huxley's 'Culture and Science' answered it in 1880).
literary_significance: The Idea of a University is the founding text of the modern debate on the purpose of higher education; its doctrine of knowledge as its own end and its portrait of the gentleman shaped the ideal of liberal education in England and America, and its argument against the purely utilitarian university is still the standard one used against vocational education.

title: Parochial and Plain Sermons
description: The sermons preached at St Mary's, Oxford, between 1828 and 1843 and published in eight volumes: the most influential body of Anglican preaching in the nineteenth century and the spiritual foundation of the Oxford Movement.
plot_or_argument: The sermons are single-argument meditations on the creed, the sacraments, sin, conscience and the unseen world, delivered to an academic congregation and designed to awaken a sense of the reality of God; the most famous, 'The Second Spring' (1852), belongs to the later Catholic collection.
historical_context: The 1830s at Oxford, the Noetics and the Oriel common room, the Evangelical revival and the High Church reaction that became the Oxford Movement.
literary_significance: The Parochial and Plain Sermons created the devotional literature of the Oxford Movement and are the finest English sermons of the century: their doctrine of the 'invisible world' and their appeal to conscience shaped Victorian religious feeling and gave the Tractarians their popular voice.

title: The Dream of Gerontius
description: Published in 1865 and set to music by Edward Elgar in 1900: a poem of the soul's journey after death, from the deathbed through judgment to purgatory, and one of the great Victorian poems on death.
plot_or_argument: Gerontius dies, his soul is borne by the guardian angel through the regions of the air, hears the demons and the angelic choirs, is presented to God and, judged, passes to the cleansing fire of purgatory with the angel's song in his ears.
historical_context: The 1860s, the Catholic doctrine of purgatory, the Victorian literature of death and the deathbed, and Newman's own old age.
literary_significance: The Dream of Gerontius is the finest Victorian poem on death and the basis of Elgar's oratorio (1900), the greatest English choral work of the century; its imagery shaped the English imagination of the afterlife and its verse carries Newman's prose cadence into poetry.

title: An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine
description: Published in 1845, in the months before Newman's reception into the Catholic Church: the argument that Catholic doctrine is the legitimate development of the original deposit of faith, and the theory that made his conversion intellectually possible.
plot_or_argument: Newman sets out the 'notes' of a true development — preservation of type, continuity of principles, power of assimilation, early anticipation, logical sequence, healing action, and chronic continuance — and tests the history of doctrine against them, concluding that the Roman Church is the legitimate heir of the early Church.
historical_context: The 1840s, the Tract 90 controversy and the Anglican crisis, and the German and French controversies over doctrinal development (Möhler, Petavius).
literary_significance: The theory of development is Newman's most original contribution to theology: it gave the Catholic Church a historical account of its own doctrine and shaped the modern ecumenical and historical theology of the twentieth century (the 'newmanian' theory is cited in the Second Vatican Council's debates).

title: The Christian Year: Thoughts in Verse for the Sundays and Holidays throughout the Year
description: Published anonymously in 1827 and the most widely read poetry book of the nineteenth century after the Bible and the hymnbook: a lyric for every Sunday and holy day of the Book of Common Prayer, written for family devotion.
plot_or_argument: Each poem takes the Gospel or Epistle of its day and turns it into a meditation — on the beauty of nature as a sign of grace, on childhood, on death, on the sacraments, and on the trusting submission of the soul to God; the sequence follows the liturgical year from Advent through Trinity and the saints' days.
literary_form: Poetry collection (109 poems, one for each Sunday and holy day)
historical_context: The 1820s-30s, the High Church devotional tradition, the Oxford of Oriel and the beginnings of the Oxford Movement, and the Victorian culture of family prayer.
literary_significance: The Christian Year was the most influential devotional poetry of the Victorian age and gave the Oxford Movement its popular voice; it shaped the spirituality of Newman and Pusey, and its Sunday-by-Sunday structure made it a permanent text of Anglican devotion and a model for later liturgical poetry.

title: Lyra Apostolica
description: Published in the British Magazine in 1833-36 and as a collection in 1836, with contributions by Keble, Newman and Richard Hurrell Froude: the poetry of the Oxford Movement's first generation, and the verse that gave the Tractarians their militant and penitential tone.
plot_or_argument: The poems are short lyrics and sonnets on the Church, the sacraments, the power of the priesthood and the corruption of the age, many of them written on the Continental tour of Newman and Froude in 1832-33.
literary_form: Poetry collection (contributions with Newman and Froude)
historical_context: The 1833 assize sermon and the founding of the Tracts, the Oxford Movement's early militancy, and the Romantic inheritance of Wordsworth and Scott in religious verse.
literary_significance: Lyra Apostolica is the primary poetic document of the Oxford Movement and the source of much of the devotional language of Victorian Anglo-Catholicism; its sonnets are among the earliest Victorian examples of the devotional sequence.

title: The Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám, the Astronomer-Poet of Persia
description: Published anonymously in 1859 in a paper wrapper at one shilling and largely ignored until Dante Gabriel Rossetti found it in 1861: the most famous English translation of Persian poetry and one of the most popular poems in the language.
plot_or_argument: The poem is a sequence of quatrains on the vanity of speculation and the urgency of present pleasure: the potter shapes the clay of dead men into pots; the Sultan and the Saint alike go down into dust; the only answer is wine and love 'here underneath the Bough, / A Jug of Wine, a Loaf of Bread — and Thou'.
literary_form: Verse translation (75 quatrains in the first edition; 101 in the fourth, 1879)
historical_context: The 1850s, the new English Orientalism and the study of Persian (Edward Cowell and the Bodleian manuscript), the Victorian crisis of faith, and the aesthetic movement's cult of melancholy pleasure.
literary_significance: The Rubáiyát is the most popular English poem of the later nineteenth century and the founding text of the vogue for Persian literature; its celebration of the present moment and its scepticism made it the philosophical poem of the 1890s aesthetic movement, and its influence on the modern English quatrain and on the decoration (Rossetti, Morris, and the Kelmscott circle) is direct.
attribution_notes: A free adaptation rather than a literal translation: FitzGerald selected, rearranged and partly invented quatrains from the Persian and constructed a continuous poem. The first edition (1859) has 75 quatrains; the fourth (1879) has 101 and is the text usually reprinted.

title: The Mighty Magician; or, The Two Ages of an Enchanter (after Calderón)
description: FitzGerald's verse translation of Calderón's drama of the magician Cyprian and the martyr Justina, privately printed in 1853 and revised as The Mighty Magician (1865): one of the earliest English translations of Calderón and a key text of the Victorian revival of Spanish drama.
plot_or_argument: Cyprian, a pagan student, sells his soul to the devil for knowledge of Justina; he is converted by her faith and both die as martyrs, and the play enacts the triumph of grace over the magical will.
literary_form: Verse drama (translation of Calderón's El mágico prodigioso)
historical_context: The 1840s-50s, the Victorian interest in Spanish drama (Lope de Vega, Calderón), and the Tractarian and Catholic revival of the period.
literary_significance: The Mighty Magician is the most important Victorian translation of Calderón and a significant document of the English revival of the Spanish Golden Age; its theme of the magician's bargain links it to Marlowe's Faustus, which FitzGerald and his circle saw as a native counterpart.

title: Euphranor: A Dialogue on Youth
description: Published in 1851, a Socratic dialogue on education set in the Cambridge of the 1830s and modelled on Plato: a discussion of what a young man should be taught and how.
plot_or_argument: Euphranor and his friends debate the aims of education, the value of mathematics and the classics, the influence of the tutor and of the family, and the formation of character; the dialogue ends without a dogmatic conclusion.
historical_context: The 1850s debates on education, the Cambridge of FitzGerald's youth, and the Victorian taste for the Platonic dialogue (Arnold's and Helps's essays).
literary_significance: Euphranor is one of the best Victorian imitations of the Platonic dialogue and a significant document for the history of English educational thought; its conviction that education is the formation of a person rather than the transmission of information is the standard Victorian humanist position.

title: The English Constitution
description: First published as essays in the Fortnightly Review in 1865-66 and collected in 1867: the most influential work of English political science and the book that taught the world how the British constitution actually works.
plot_or_argument: Bagehot distinguishes the 'dignified' parts of the constitution — the monarchy and the House of Lords — whose function is to make government intelligible and acceptable to the people, from the 'efficient' parts — the cabinet, the House of Commons and the civil service — which actually govern; he then analyses the cabinet as a 'committee' of the legislature, the role of the Commons, the House of Lords, the monarchy and the change introduced by the Reform Act of 1867.
historical_context: The 1860s, the Second Reform Act of 1867, the American Civil War and the comparison with the American presidency, and the new political journalism of the Fortnightly and the Economist.
literary_significance: The English Constitution is the founding work of modern comparative political science: the 'dignified' and 'efficient' distinction is still the standard analysis of constitutional monarchy, and the book taught the nineteenth-century world how the British system worked. Its analysis of the cabinet and of the civil service shaped the study of government in Britain and the United States.

title: Physics and Politics; or, Thoughts on the Application of the Principles of 'Natural Selection' and 'Inheritance' to Political Society
description: Published in 1872 and first given as essays in the Fortnightly Review: the founding English work of social evolutionism, and an early attempt to apply Darwinian theory to the development of nations and to the question of why some societies progress and others do not.
plot_or_argument: Bagehot argues that progress depends on the 'cake of custom' being broken by a 'preliminary age of discussion', that the 'nation-making' period precedes the 'nation-keeping' one, and that the 'verifiable progress' of modern societies depends on the spread of the 'discussion' that only free institutions permit.
historical_context: The 1860s-70s, the Darwinian revolution and the rise of social Darwinism, the unification of Germany and Italy, and the debate on the 'Aryan' and 'savage' races.
literary_significance: Physics and Politics founded the evolutionary study of politics and introduced the idea of the 'age of discussion' as the mechanism of progress; it is a key text for the history of social Darwinism and for the modern critique of the Victorian idea of progress, and it influenced the sociology of Spencer, Maine and the American social scientists.

title: Lombard Street: A Description of the Money Market
description: Published in 1873 and the classic English account of the money market: a description of how the Bank of England, the bill brokers and the joint-stock banks actually worked, and an argument for the Bank's responsibility as the holder of the ultimate reserve.
plot_or_argument: Bagehot describes the structure of the London money market, the role of the discount houses and the bill brokers, the 'one reserve' system of the Bank of England and the panic of 1866, and argues that in a crisis the Bank must lend freely at a high rate against good security — the 'lender of last resort' doctrine.
historical_context: The 1866 collapse of Overend, Gurney and Co. and the panic that followed, the gold standard, and the Victorian debate on banking reform after the 1844 Act.
literary_significance: Lombard Street is the founding text of modern central banking: the 'lender of last resort' doctrine is still the basis of central bank behaviour in a crisis, and Bagehot's description of the money market is the classic account of how credit works. It shaped the Federal Reserve's response to the panics of the twentieth century and the 2008 crisis.

title: The English Constitution (Introduction to the Second Edition)
description: The long introduction added to the second edition of 1872, in which Bagehot revised his account of the constitution after the Reform Act of 1867 and the rise of the 'working man' as a political force.
plot_or_argument: Bagehot argues that the 1867 Act has made the House of Commons the real sovereign, that the 'theatrical' elements of the constitution have lost their hold on the new electorate, and that the 'efficient' parts must now be explained to a democratic public.
historical_context: The 1867 Reform Act, the 1868 election and the first working-class MPs, and the debate on the future of the House of Lords.
literary_significance: The 1872 introduction is a foundational text for the study of the democratisation of British politics and the decline of the 'dignified' constitution; it is the classic statement of the shift from the mid-Victorian 'deferential' politics to the mass politics of the later century.
